<!-- maintheorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
There is an absolute constant $C\geq1$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-distance}
 C^{-1}\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P)}(f,\mathcal A)
 \leq \lVert Df\rVert_{L^1(\mathbb P^{\otimes3})}
 \leq 4\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P)}(f,\mathcal A)
 \qquad(f\in L^1(\mathbb P)).
\end{equation}
Consequently $\ker D=\mathcal A$, and the map
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-J}
 J:L^1(\mathbb P)/R\longrightarrow
 \mathbb R\oplus_1 L^1(\mathbb P^{\otimes3}),
 \qquad J(f+R)\coloneqq(\mathbb E f,Df),
\end{equation}
is well defined and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-J-bounds}
 \frac{1}{2C}\lVert f+R\rVert_{L^1/R}
 \leq \lVert J(f+R)\rVert
 \leq 5\lVert f+R\rVert_{L^1/R}.
\end{equation}
Both $L^1(\mathbb P)/R$ and $L^1(\mathbb P)/\mathcal A$ therefore embed into $L^1(0,1)$. One admissible value of $C$ is given in \eqref{eq:constants} below.
<!-- end maintheorem-1 -->
<!-- maintheorem-2: body_md -->
\label{c:thm:mainnorm}
For every $T\in\mathscr B(X)$,
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:mainnorm}
 \lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert\leq\lVert T\rVert_w\leq2\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert.
\end{equation}
Thus $[T]\mapsto T^{\mathrm{co}}$ is an injective homomorphism with closed range and inverse norm at most $2$ on its image.
<!-- end maintheorem-2 -->
<!-- maintheorem-3: body_md -->
\label{c:thm:mainalgebra}
The algebra $\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X)$ is uniformly incompressible.
Let $C$ be the constant in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
For every normed algebra $B$ and every bounded injective homomorphism $\Phi:\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X)\to B$,
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:mainalgebra}
 \lVert \Phi(a)\rVert\geq
 \frac{\lVert a\rVert}{40C\lVert \Phi\rVert^2}
 \qquad(a\in\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end maintheorem-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:integration-tools}
Let $(S,\Sigma,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\Sigma$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra.
For $h\in L^1(P)$, there is a unique $\mathcal G$-measurable element of $L^1(P)$, denoted by $\mathbb E[h\mid\mathcal G]$, such that
\[
 \int_A\mathbb E[h\mid\mathcal G]\,dP=\int_Ah\,dP
 \qquad(A\in\mathcal G).
\]
Uniqueness is understood modulo null sets. Conditional expectation is linear, positive, preserves integrals, and fixes $\mathcal G$-measurable functions.
For $h\in L^p(P)$, $1\leq p<\infty$, conditional Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 |\mathbb E[h\mid\mathcal G]|^p\leq\mathbb E[|h|^p\mid\mathcal G]
 \quad\text{almost everywhere}.
\]
Consequently $\lVert \mathbb E[h\mid\mathcal G]\rVert_p\leq\lVert h\rVert_p$ for $1\leq p\leq\infty$.
On a product probability space, conditioning on one factor amounts to integrating over the other factor.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:Bernoulli-law}
There is a probability measure $\mathbb P$ on $\Delta=\{-1,1\}^{\mathbb N}$, with its product $\sigma$-algebra, such that
\[
 \mathbb P\{x:x_j=\varepsilon_j\ (j\in F)\}=2^{-|F|}
 \quad(F\subset\mathbb N\text{ finite},\ \varepsilon_j\in\{-1,1\}).
\]
Its coordinate functions are independent fair signs. More generally, measurable functions depending on disjoint coordinate sets are independent.
Explicitly, if $g:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and $f(x)\coloneqq g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, then
\[
 \int_\Delta f(x)\,d\mathbb P(x)
 =2^{-n}\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^n}g(\varepsilon).
\]
This is the Bernoulli instance of the product-measure construction; see \cite[Theorem~A.3.1, Example~A.3.2, and Theorems~2.1.11--2.1.13]{Dur19}.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Push Lebesgue measure on $[0,1)$ forward under the binary-digit map $t\mapsto((-1)^{\beta_j(t)})_j$. Dyadic intervals show that the first $n$ signs have the uniform distribution; summing over unspecified signs gives the displayed formula. Independence follows first for cylinders and then for the generated $\sigma$-algebras by the monotone-class theorem.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:distribution-tools}
Let $Z\geq0$ be integrable and put $a(t)\coloneqq\mathbb P(Z>t)$.
Markov's inequality and the layer-cake formula \cite[Theorem~1.6.4 and Exercise~1.7.2]{Dur19} give, for $t,M>0$,
\[
 a(t)\leq\frac{\mathbb E Z}{t},\qquad
 \mathbb E Z=\int_0^\infty a(t)\,dt,\qquad
 \mathbb E[Z\mathbf1_{\{Z>M\}}]=Ma(M)+\int_M^\infty a(t)\,dt.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The first assertion follows from $t\mathbf1_{\{Z>t\}}\leq Z$. For the others, integrate the pointwise identities
\[
 Z=\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{Z>t\}}\,dt,\qquad
 Z\mathbf1_{\{Z>M\}}=M\mathbf1_{\{Z>M\}}+
 \int_M^\infty\mathbf1_{\{Z>t\}}\,dt
\]
using Tonelli's theorem. We also use the finite union bound in its pointwise form $\mathbf1_{\cup_j A_j}\leq\sum_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:mixed-interpolation}
For $1\leq p\leq q<\infty$ and measurable $h$ on a product of probability spaces,
\[
 \lVert h\rVert_{L^q_t(L^p_x)}\leq\lVert h\rVert_{L^p_x(L^q_t)}.
\]
On a probability space, $\lVert h\rVert_p\leq\lVert h\rVert_q$ for $p\leq q$. The further estimates used below are
\[
 \lVert h\rVert_{5/4}\leq\lVert h\rVert_\infty^{1/5}\lVert h\rVert_1^{4/5},
 \qquad
 \lVert h\rVert_2\leq\lVert h\rVert_1^{1/3}\lVert h\rVert_4^{2/3}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Put $s=q/p\geq1$. The integral triangle inequality in $L^s_t$ gives
\[
 \lVert h\rVert_{L^q_t(L^p_x)}^p
 =\left\lVert\int |h(x,\cdot)|^p\,dP(x)\right\rVert_{L^s_t}
 \leq\int\lVert |h(x,\cdot)|^p\rVert_{L^s_t}\,dP(x)
 =\lVert h\rVert_{L^p_x(L^q_t)}^p.
\]
The norm comparison follows from H\"older's inequality and $P(S)=1$. Integrating $|h|^{5/4}\leq\lVert h\rVert_\infty^{1/4}|h|$ proves the first interpolation estimate. Applying H\"older with exponents $3/2$ and $3$ to $|h|^2=|h|^{2/3}|h|^{4/3}$ proves the second.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:coupling}
Let $U_i:\Delta_n^3\to\Delta_n$, $0\leq i\leq3$, be the maps defined above on the probability space $(\Delta_n^3,Q_n)$.
For every $u,v\in\Delta_n$, the following identities hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Each marginal is uniform:
\[
 Q_n(U_i=u)=2^{-n}\qquad(0\leq i\leq3).
\]
\item The pairs $(U_0,U_1)$ and $(U_2,U_3)$ are independent:
\[
 Q_n(U_i=u,U_j=v)=2^{-2n}
 \qquad((i,j)\in\{(0,1),(2,3)\}).
\]
\item For $(i,j)\in\{(0,2),(0,3),(1,2),(1,3)\}$,
\[
 Q_n(U_j=v\mid U_i=u)
 =\prod_{k=1}^n\left(\tfrac34\mathbf1_{\{v_k=u_k\}}+
                     \tfrac14\mathbf1_{\{v_k=-u_k\}}\right).
\]
Thus, conditionally on $U_i=u$, the coordinates of $U_j$ are independent, with $Q_n((U_j)_k=u_k\mid U_i=u)=3/4$.
The same formula holds with $i$ and $j$ interchanged.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For a fixed $\sigma$, the transformation $(x,y)\mapsto(z,w)$ permutes the two entries in each coordinate and preserves $\mathbb P_n\otimes\mathbb P_n$. This proves the assertion about $(z,w)$ and hence all marginal assertions. The independence of $(x,y)$ is part of the construction.

For example, conditionally on $x$, the variable $z_j$ equals $x_j$ if $\sigma_j=1$; if $\sigma_j=-1$, it is the independent fair sign $y_j$. Therefore
\[
 Q_n(z_j=x_j\mid x)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac34.
\]
The pairs $(y_j,\sigma_j)$ are independent over $j$, giving the product conditional law. Interchanging $x,y$ or $z,w$ proves the other three cases. The product on the right-hand side of (iii) is symmetric in the two points. Together with their equal uniform marginals, this proves the same conditional formula with the two points interchanged.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:adjoint}
For $1\leq p\leq\infty$ and $f\in L^p(\Delta_n,\mathbb P_n)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D-bounded}
 \lVert D_nf\rVert_p\leq4\lVert f\rVert_p,
 \qquad D_na=0\quad(a\in\mathcal A_n).
\end{equation}
Let $D_n^\dagger$ denote the Hilbert-space adjoint for the normalized $L^2$ inner products. Its finite-dimensional formula defines an operator from $L^p(\Delta_n^3,Q_n)$ to $L^p(\Delta_n,\mathbb P_n)$ and, for every $v\in L^p(\Delta_n^3,Q_n)$, satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjoint-bound}
 \lVert D_n^\dagger v\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb P_n)}
 \leq4\lVert v\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb P_n^{\otimes3})}.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal}
 D_n^\dagger D_n=4(I+P_0-2T).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Fix $1\leq p\leq\infty$. For $0\leq i\leq3$, define
\[
 C_i:L^p(\Delta_n,\mathbb P_n)\longrightarrow L^p(\Delta_n^3,Q_n),
 \qquad C_i f\coloneqq f\circ U_i.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:coupling}, $\lVert C_i f\rVert_{L^p(Q_n)}=\lVert f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb P_n)}$ for every $f\in L^p(\Delta_n,\mathbb P_n)$.
Consequently
\[
 D_n=C_0+C_1-C_2-C_3,\qquad
 \lVert D_nf\rVert_{L^p(Q_n)}\leq\sum_{i=0}^3\lVert C_i f\rVert_{L^p(Q_n)}
 =4\lVert f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb P_n)}.
\]
The identities $D_n\mathbf 1=0$ and $D_nr_j=0$ follow from $x_j+y_j=z_j+w_j$.

Define
\[
 F_i:L^p(\Delta_n^3,Q_n)\longrightarrow L^p(\Delta_n,\mathbb P_n)
\]
by the following formula, for $v\in L^p(\Delta_n^3,Q_n)$:
\[
 (F_i v)(u)\coloneqq
 2^{-2n}\sum_{\substack{\omega\in\Delta_n^3\\U_i(\omega)=u}}v(\omega)
 =\mathbb E_{Q_n}[v\mid U_i=u]\qquad(u\in\Delta_n).
\]
The fiber has $2^{2n}$ elements because $U_i$ is uniform. Since $U_i$ has distribution $\mathbb P_n$, Jensen's inequality gives $\lVert F_i v\rVert_p\leq\lVert v\rVert_p$ for $1\leq p<\infty$; the supremum-norm estimate follows directly from the averaging formula. The normalized inner products are
\[
 \langle f,g\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P_n)}\coloneqq\int_{\Delta_n}fg\,d\mathbb P_n,
 \qquad
 \langle v,w\rangle_{L^2(Q_n)}\coloneqq\int_{\Delta_n^3}vw\,dQ_n.
\]
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb P_n)$ and $v\in L^2(Q_n)$, direct integration gives
\[
 \langle C_i f,v\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P_n^{\otimes3})}
 =\langle f,F_i v\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb P_n)}.
\]
Thus $D_n^\dagger=F_0+F_1-F_2-F_3$, proving \eqref{eq:adjoint-bound}.

To compute the normal operator, expand
\[
 D_n^\dagger D_n=\sum_{i,j=0}^3s_i s_j F_i C_j.
\]
The four terms with $i=j$ give $4I$. The four ordered pairs obtained from $(0,1)$ and $(2,3)$ give $4P_0$, since those points are independent and $s_i=s_j$. Each of the eight remaining ordered pairs gives $-T_{1/2}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:coupling}. This proves \eqref{eq:normal}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:finite-kernel}
One has $\ker D_n=\mathcal A_n$. More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal-spectrum}
 D_n^\dagger D_n w_S=
 \begin{cases}
 0,& |S|=0\text{ or }1,\\
 4(1-2^{1-|S|})w_S,& |S|\geq2.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
All nonzero eigenvalues in this formula are at least $2$.
These are eigenvalues of the endomorphism $D_n^\dagger D_n$ of $L^2(\mathbb P_n)$.
The operator $D_n$ itself has a different target space, so this is not an eigenvalue assertion for $D_n$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Apply \eqref{eq:normal} to the Walsh basis using \eqref{eq:noise-spectrum}. Since $\lVert D_nf\rVert_2^2=\langle D_n^\dagger D_nf,f\rangle$, the kernel is precisely the sum of Walsh levels zero and one.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:HC}
For $1<p\leq2$ and $0\leq\Theta\leq\sqrt{p-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HC}
 \lVert T_\Theta u\rVert_{L^2(\mathbb P_n)}\leq\lVert u\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb P_n)}
 \qquad(u:\Delta_n\to\mathbb R).
\end{equation}
The constant is $1$ for every $n$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:HC-special}
 \lVert T_{1/2}u\rVert_2\leq\lVert u\rVert_{5/4},
 \qquad
 \lVert T_{1/\sqrt2}u\rVert_2\leq\lVert u\rVert_{3/2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:two-point}
For $1<p\leq2$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-point}
 a^2+(p-1)b^2
 \leq\left(\frac{|a+b|^p+|a-b|^p}{2}\right)^{2/p}.
\end{equation}
Consequently the one-coordinate noise operator satisfies
\[
 \lVert T_{\sqrt{p-1}}u\rVert_{L^2(\{-1,1\})}
 \leq\lVert u\rVert_{L^p(\{-1,1\})}
\]
for $u:\{-1,1\}\to\mathbb R$, with normalized counting measure.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The case $p=2$ is an identity, with noise operator $T_1=I$. Suppose $1<p<2$. If $a=0$, then \eqref{eq:two-point} follows from $p-1\leq1$. Assume $a\ne0$ and set
\[
 A(t)\coloneqq\frac{|a+t|^p+|a-t|^p}{2},
 \qquad F(t)\coloneqq A(t)^{2/p}.
\]
The function $A$ is strictly positive. Away from $t=\pm a$, differentiation gives
\[
 A''(t)=p(p-1)\frac{|a+t|^{p-2}+|a-t|^{p-2}}2
\]
and
\begin{align*}
 F''(t)
 &=\frac2p\left(\frac2p-1\right)A(t)^{2/p-2}(A'(t))^2
   +\frac2p A(t)^{2/p-1}A''(t)\\
 &\geq2(p-1)A(t)^{(2-p)/p}
       \frac{|a+t|^{p-2}+|a-t|^{p-2}}2.
\end{align*}
The function $s\mapsto s^{(p-2)/p}$ is convex on $(0,\infty)$, so its defining midpoint convexity inequality shows that the final product, without the factor $2(p-1)$, is at least $1$. Hence $F''(t)\geq2(p-1)$ wherever the displayed derivatives are finite.

The derivative $F'$ is locally absolutely continuous. Indeed, the possible singularities in $A''$ have order $|t\mp a|^{p-2}$, which is locally integrable because $p>1$, and $A$ is bounded away from zero on compact intervals. Since $F(0)=a^2$, $F'(0)=0$, and $F'$ is locally absolutely continuous, for $t\geq0$ we have
\[
 F(t)=F(0)+tF'(0)+\int_0^t(t-s)F''(s)\,ds
 \geq a^2+(p-1)t^2.
\]
The second derivative is used only almost everywhere, so this identity also crosses the two possible singular points.
Evenness of $F$ and $t=|b|$ prove \eqref{eq:two-point}.

For a real function $u$ on $\{-1,1\}$ write $u(\epsilon)=a+b\epsilon$. Its noisy version is $a+\sqrt{p-1}\,b\epsilon$, whose squared $L^2$ norm is the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:two-point}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Fix $1<p\leq2$ and first take $\Theta=\sqrt{p-1}$. The one-coordinate assertion is Lemma~\ref{lem:two-point}. Suppose the assertion is known on $\Delta_{n-1}$. Write the variables as $(u,t)\in\Delta_{n-1}\times\{-1,1\}$, and define
\begin{align*}
 (Vf)(u,t)&\coloneqq\frac{1+\Theta}{2}f(u,t)
                  +\frac{1-\Theta}{2}f(u,-t),\\
 (Sf)(u,t)&\coloneqq\int_{\Delta_{n-1}}f(u\odot\epsilon,t)
                         \,d\nu_{n-1,\Theta}(\epsilon).
\end{align*}
Thus $V$ averages function values in the last coordinate while $S$ does so in the first $n-1$ coordinates.
The product identity $\nu_{n,\Theta}=\nu_{n-1,\Theta}\otimes\nu_{1,\Theta}$ and Fubini give $SV=VS=T_\Theta$ on $\Delta_n$.

Apply the induction hypothesis for each fixed $t$, then the mixed-norm inequality in Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-interpolation} (since $p\leq2$), and finally the one-coordinate inequality for each fixed $u$:
\begin{align*}
 \lVert SVf\rVert_{L^2_t(L^2_u)}
 &\leq\lVert Vf\rVert_{L^2_t(L^p_u)}\\
 &\leq\lVert Vf\rVert_{L^p_u(L^2_t)}\\
 &\leq\lVert f\rVert_{L^p_u(L^p_t)}
 =\lVert f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb P_n)}.
\end{align*}
All norms here use probability measures. This proves the assertion at $\Theta=\sqrt{p-1}$ for every $n$. If $0\leq\Theta\leq\sqrt{p-1}$, use
\[
 T_\Theta=T_{\Theta/\sqrt{p-1}}T_{\sqrt{p-1}}
\]
and the $L^2$ contractivity of the first factor. This proves \eqref{eq:HC}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:Lp}
For every $n$ and $f:\Delta_n\to\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lp-estimate}
 \lVert f-\Pi_nf\rVert_{5/4}\leq5\lVert D_nf\rVert_{5/4}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lp-distance}
 \operatorname{dist}_{L^{5/4}(\mathbb P_n)}(f,\mathcal A_n)\leq5\lVert D_nf\rVert_{5/4}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Set $h=f-\Pi_nf$ and $g=D_n^\dagger D_nf$. The function $h$ has only Walsh levels of degree at least two. Since $D_n\Pi_nf=0$ and $P_0h=0$, formula \eqref{eq:normal} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:g-h}
 g=4(I-2T)h.
\end{equation}
On each Walsh level of degree $k\geq2$, the multiplier $4(1-2^{1-k})$ is at least $2$. The operators in \eqref{eq:g-h} commute with $T$. Parseval's identity therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smoothed-spectral}
 \lVert Th\rVert_2\leq\tfrac12\lVert Tg\rVert_2
 \leq\tfrac12\lVert g\rVert_{5/4},
\end{equation}
where the last step is \eqref{eq:HC-special}. Solving \eqref{eq:g-h} for $h$ gives $h=g/4+2Th$. Since the underlying measure is a probability measure,
\begin{align*}
 \lVert h\rVert_{5/4}
 &\leq\tfrac14\lVert g\rVert_{5/4}+2\lVert Th\rVert_{5/4}\\
 &\leq\tfrac14\lVert g\rVert_{5/4}+2\lVert Th\rVert_2
 \leq\tfrac54\lVert g\rVert_{5/4}
 \leq5\lVert D_nf\rVert_{5/4},
\end{align*}
using \eqref{eq:adjoint-bound} in the last step. The distance estimate follows by using $\Pi_nf\in\mathcal A_n$ as an approximant.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-L1-Q}
No uniform $L^1$ bound for $\Pi_n$ is assumed or deduced. The estimate just proved applies in $L^{5/4}$. The $L^1$ argument below works with the quotient distance, not with $\lVert f-\Pi_nf\rVert_1$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:small-sets}
For every $B\subseteq\Delta_n$ and all distinct $i,j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:small-sets}
 Q_n(U_i\in B,\ U_j\in B)\leq\mathbb P_n(B)^{4/3}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For the independent pairs in Lemma~\ref{lem:coupling}, the left-hand side is $\mathbb P_n(B)^2$, which is at most $\mathbb P_n(B)^{4/3}$. For any of the other pairs it equals
\begin{align*}
 \langle \mathbf 1_B,T_{1/2}\mathbf 1_B\rangle
 &=\lVert T_{1/\sqrt2}\mathbf 1_B\rVert_2^2\\
 &\leq\lVert \mathbf 1_B\rVert_{3/2}^2=\mathbb P_n(B)^{4/3}.
\end{align*}
Here $T_{1/2}=T_{1/\sqrt2}T_{1/\sqrt2}$ and self-adjointness give the equality.
For the inequality, use $p=3/2$ and $\Theta=1/\sqrt2=\sqrt{p-1}$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:HC}.
Finally, $\lVert \mathbf 1_B\rVert_{3/2}=\mathbb P_n(B)^{2/3}$, giving the exponent $4/3$ after squaring.
In general, the same argument gives
\[
 \int\mathbf 1_BT_\Theta\mathbf 1_B\,d\mathbb P_n
 \leq\mathbb P_n(B)^{2/(1+\Theta)}\quad(0\leq\Theta\leq1):
\]
for $\Theta>0$ take $p=1+\Theta$ and use $T_\Theta=T_{\sqrt\Theta}^2$; for $\Theta=0$, use $T_0=P_0$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:tail}
Let $f:\Delta_n\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lVert f\rVert_1=1$, and put $\varepsilon=\lVert D_nf\rVert_1$. Then for every $M>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail}
 \int_{\{|f|>M\}}|f|\,d\mathbb P_n
 \leq2\varepsilon+\gamma M^{-1/3},
 \qquad \gamma=6^{7/3}.
\end{equation}
The estimate is independent of $n$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Define
\[
 a(t)\coloneqq\mathbb P_n\{|f|>t\}\quad(t>0),
 \qquad Z_i\coloneqq|f(U_i)|\quad(0\leq i\leq3).
\]
The distribution identities in Lemma~\ref{lem:distribution-tools} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:distribution}
 a(t)\leq t^{-1},\qquad \int_0^\infty a(t)\,d t=1.
\end{equation}
Each $Z_i$ has this same tail distribution. We do not assume that these four random variables are independent.

On the event
\[
 Z_0>M,\qquad Z_j\leq Z_0/6\quad(j=1,2,3),
\]
the reverse triangle inequality gives
\[
 |D_nf|\geq Z_0-Z_1-Z_2-Z_3\geq Z_0/2.
\]
Splitting off this event and using the union bound on its complement yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-split}
 \mathbb E_{Q_n}[Z_0\mathbf 1_{\{Z_0>M\}}]
 \leq2\varepsilon+
 \sum_{j=1}^3\mathbb E_{Q_n}[Z_0\mathbf 1_{\{Z_0>M,\ Z_j>Z_0/6\}}].
\end{equation}
For $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ set $V_j\coloneqq\min(Z_0,6Z_j)$. On the event appearing in the $j$th summand, $V_j=Z_0>M$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:min-domination}
 \mathbb E_{Q_n}[Z_0\mathbf 1_{\{Z_0>M,\ Z_j>Z_0/6\}}]
 \leq\mathbb E_{Q_n}[V_j\mathbf 1_{\{V_j>M\}}].
\end{equation}
For every $t>0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:small-sets}, applied to the \emph{same} level set at threshold $t/6$, gives
\begin{align}
 Q_n(V_j>t)
 &=Q_n(Z_0>t,\ Z_j>t/6)\notag\\
 &\leq Q_n(Z_0>t/6,\ Z_j>t/6)
 \leq a(t/6)^{4/3}.\label{eq:min-tail}
\end{align}
The truncated layer-cake identity, followed by \eqref{eq:min-tail}, shows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:layer-min}
 \mathbb E_{Q_n}[V_j\mathbf 1_{\{V_j>M\}}]
 \leq M a(M/6)^{4/3}+\int_M^\infty a(t/6)^{4/3}\,d t.
\end{equation}
The first term is at most $6^{4/3}M^{-1/3}$ by \eqref{eq:distribution}. For $t\geq M$, the same estimate gives
\[
 a(t/6)^{4/3}\leq(6/M)^{1/3}a(t/6).
\]
Therefore the integral in \eqref{eq:layer-min} is at most
\[
 (6/M)^{1/3}\int_M^\infty a(t/6)\,d t
 =6(6/M)^{1/3}\int_{M/6}^\infty a(s)\,d s
 \leq6^{4/3}M^{-1/3}.
\]
Each of the three summands in \eqref{eq:tail-split} is consequently bounded by $2\cdot6^{4/3}M^{-1/3}$. Summation proves \eqref{eq:tail}, because $3\cdot2\cdot6^{4/3}=6^{7/3}$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:homogeneous-tail}
Rescaling gives the homogeneous form
\[
 \int_{\{|f|>M\lVert f\rVert_1\}}|f|\,d\mathbb P_n
 \leq2\lVert D_nf\rVert_1+\gamma M^{-1/3}\lVert f\rVert_1
\]
for nonzero $f$. The tail estimate applies to all functions, not only to functions orthogonal to $\mathcal A_n$. For affine functions the defect vanishes, which is consistent with their uniformly controlled tails after $L^1$ normalization.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:finite-endpoint}
For every $n\geq1$ and $f:\Delta_n\to\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-endpoint}
 \operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(f,\mathcal A_n)\leq C\lVert D_nf\rVert_1.
\end{equation}
Together with \eqref{eq:D-bounded}, this gives
\[
 C^{-1}\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(f,\mathcal A_n)
 \leq\lVert D_nf\rVert_1
 \leq4\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(f,\mathcal A_n).
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Write $d=\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(f,\mathcal A_n)$. If $d=0$, the assertion is immediate. Otherwise, a best approximant $a_*\in\mathcal A_n$ exists. Indeed, a minimizing sequence in $\mathcal A_n$ is bounded by the triangle inequality; finite dimensionality gives a convergent subsequence. Replacing $f$ by $(f-a_*)/d$, and using $D_na_*=0$, reduces the proof to the normalization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalization}
 \lVert f\rVert_1=\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(f,\mathcal A_n)=1.
\end{equation}
Set $\varepsilon=\lVert D_nf\rVert_1$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-kernel}, $\varepsilon>0$. If $\varepsilon\geq1$, then $1\leq C\varepsilon$. It remains to consider $0<\varepsilon\leq1$.

Choose
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cutoff}
 M=\varepsilon^{-3},\qquad
 b=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\leq M\}},\qquad
 \delta=\lVert f-b\rVert_1.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:tail} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta}
 \delta\leq2\varepsilon+\gamma M^{-1/3}
 =A_0\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
By boundedness of $D_n$ and the pointwise bound on $b$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Db-endpoints}
 \lVert D_nb\rVert_1\leq\varepsilon+4\delta
 \leq(1+4A_0)\varepsilon,
 \qquad \lVert D_nb\rVert_\infty\leq4M.
\end{equation}
For any bounded function $v$ on a probability space,
\[
 \lVert v\rVert_{5/4}\leq\lVert v\rVert_\infty^{1/5}\lVert v\rVert_1^{4/5};
\]
this follows directly by integrating $|v|^{5/4}\leq\lVert v\rVert_\infty^{1/4}|v|$. Thus \eqref{eq:Db-endpoints} and \eqref{eq:cutoff} imply
\begin{align}
 \lVert D_nb\rVert_{5/4}
 &\leq (4\varepsilon^{-3})^{1/5}
       ((1+4A_0)\varepsilon)^{4/5}\notag\\
 &=4^{1/5}(1+4A_0)^{4/5}\varepsilon^{1/5}.
 \label{eq:Db-Lp}
\end{align}
Using \eqref{eq:normalization}, the triangle inequality for distance, and Proposition~\ref{prop:Lp}, we obtain
\begin{align}
 1
 &\leq\lVert f-b\rVert_1+\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(b,\mathcal A_n)\notag\\
 &\leq\delta+\operatorname{dist}_{L^{5/4}(\mathbb P_n)}(b,\mathcal A_n)\notag\\
 &\leq A_0\varepsilon
      +5\cdot4^{1/5}(1+4A_0)^{4/5}\varepsilon^{1/5}
 \leq B_0\varepsilon^{1/5}.
 \label{eq:absorption}
\end{align}
The second line uses $\lVert u\rVert_1\leq\lVert u\rVert_{5/4}$ for each candidate residual $u=b-a$. The final step uses $\varepsilon\leq1$. It follows that $\varepsilon\geq B_0^{-5}=C^{-1}$. Undoing the normalization gives \eqref{eq:finite-endpoint}.

For the upper estimate, apply $\lVert D_n(f-a)\rVert_1\leq4\lVert f-a\rVert_1$ to each $a\in\mathcal A_n$ and take the infimum.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:conditional}
The maps $E_n$ are contractions on $L^1(\mathbb P)$, and $E_nf\to f$ in $L^1(\mathbb P)$ for each $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conditional-A}
 E_nR=\operatorname{span}\{r_1,\ldots,r_n\},\qquad E_n\mathcal A=\mathcal A_n.
\end{equation}
For every $\mathcal F_n$-measurable $u$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:distance-reflection}
 \operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P)}(u,\mathcal A)
 =\operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P_n)}(u,\mathcal A_n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Contractivity is Jensen's inequality. Finite-coordinate cylinder sets form an algebra generating the product $\sigma$-algebra. The monotone-class theorem and dominated convergence therefore imply that cylinder functions are dense in $L^1(\mathbb P)$. Given a cylinder function $v$ depending on the first $m$ coordinates, $E_nv=v$ for $n\geq m$; consequently
\[
 \lVert E_nf-f\rVert_1\leq2\lVert f-v\rVert_1\qquad(n\geq m).
\]
Density proves convergence.

Independence gives $E_nr_j=r_j$ if $j\leq n$, and $E_nr_j=0$ if $j>n$. By continuity and finite-dimensional closedness, $E_nR$ is contained in the indicated span. The reverse inclusion follows because $E_n$ fixes that span. The assertion about $\mathcal A$ follows as well.

Since $\mathcal A_n\subseteq\mathcal A$, the left side of \eqref{eq:distance-reflection} is at most the right side. Conversely, for any $a\in\mathcal A$, the element $E_na$ belongs to $\mathcal A_n$, and
\[
 \lVert u-E_na\rVert_1=\lVert E_n(u-a)\rVert_1\leq\lVert u-a\rVert_1.
\]
Taking infima proves the reverse inequality. The $L^1$ norm of a cylinder function agrees exactly with its norm on the finite cube.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:infinite-D}
Formula \eqref{eq:D-infinite} defines a bounded linear operator
\[
 D:L^1(\mathbb P)\longrightarrow L^1(\mathbb P^{\otimes3})
\]
of norm at most $4$. It vanishes on $\mathcal A$. If $u$ depends on the first $n$ coordinates, then $Du$ is the corresponding cylinder realization of $D_nu$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cylinder-D}
 \lVert Du\rVert_{L^1(\mathbb P^{\otimes3})}
 =\lVert D_nu\rVert_{L^1(\mathbb P_n^{\otimes3})}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The coordinate maps in \eqref{eq:swaps} are measurable. All four points $x,y,z,w$ have distribution $\mathbb P$: this follows from their finite-dimensional distributions, or directly from the coordinatewise construction. Pullback along each of these four maps therefore preserves the $L^1$ norm. It also respects equivalence classes, since the inverse image of a $\mathbb P$-null set is $\mathbb P^{\otimes3}$-null. Formula \eqref{eq:D-infinite} therefore defines $D$ with norm at most $4$.

The identities $D\mathbf 1=0$ and $Dr_j=0$, followed by continuity and \eqref{eq:spaces}, show that $D$ vanishes on $\mathcal A$. For cylinder functions the defining formula uses only the corresponding finite coordinates, proving \eqref{eq:cylinder-D}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:infinite-distance}
The estimate \eqref{eq:main-distance} holds, and $\ker D=\mathcal A$. In particular,
\[
 \widetilde D:L^1(\mathbb P)/\mathcal A\longrightarrow L^1(\mathbb P^{\otimes3}),
 \qquad \widetilde D(f+\mathcal A)=Df,
\]
is an isomorphism onto a closed subspace, with $\lVert \widetilde D\rVert\leq4$ and $\lVert \widetilde D^{-1}\rVert\leq C$ on its range.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-endpoint} to $f_n=E_nf$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:conditional} and~\ref{lem:infinite-D},
\[
 \operatorname{dist}_{L^1(\mathbb P)}(f_n,\mathcal A)\leq C\lVert Df_n\rVert_1.
\]
As $n\to\infty$, we have $f_n\to f$ and $Df_n\to Df$ in their respective $L^1$ spaces. Distance to a fixed subset is $1$-Lipschitz, so the lower bound in \eqref{eq:main-distance} follows. The upper bound follows by subtracting any $a\in\mathcal A$, since $Da=0$.

Closedness of $\mathcal A$ and the lower bound identify the kernel. The induced map has the stated two-sided bounds. A bounded-below operator from a Banach space has closed range, which proves the remaining assertion.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:J}
The map $J$ in \eqref{eq:main-J} is well defined and satisfies \eqref{eq:main-J-bounds}. Its range is closed.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Both the mean and $D$ vanish on $R$, so $J$ is well defined and linear. For every $r\in R$,
\[
 |\mathbb E f|\leq\lVert f-r\rVert_1,
 \qquad \lVert Df\rVert_1=\lVert D(f-r)\rVert_1\leq4\lVert f-r\rVert_1.
\]
Taking the infimum gives $\lVert J(f+R)\rVert\leq5\lVert f+R\rVert_{L^1/R}$.

For $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r\in R$, write $u=f-c\mathbf 1-r$. Since $\mathbb E r=0$,
\[
 |c|=|\mathbb E f-\mathbb E u|\leq|\mathbb E f|+\lVert u\rVert_1.
\]
Hence
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(f,R)\leq\lVert f-r\rVert_1\leq|\mathbb E f|+2\lVert u\rVert_1.
\]
Infimizing over $c\mathbf 1+r\in\mathcal A$ and using Proposition~\ref{prop:infinite-distance}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mean-recovery}
 \operatorname{dist}(f,R)\leq|\mathbb E f|+2\operatorname{dist}(f,\mathcal A)
 \leq|\mathbb E f|+2C\lVert Df\rVert_1
 \leq2C\lVert J(f+R)\rVert.
\end{equation}
Here $C\geq1$. This is the lower estimate in \eqref{eq:main-J-bounds}, and it also implies closedness of the range.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:R-Hilbert}
The coefficient map $(a_j)\mapsto\sum_j a_jr_j$ extends to an isomorphism from $\ell_2(\mathbb R)$ onto $R$. More precisely, for every finitely supported scalar sequence,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Khintchine-rough}
 \frac1{\sqrt3}\Bigl(\sum_j|a_j|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}
 \leq\left\lVert\sum_j a_jr_j\right\rVert_1
 \leq\Bigl(\sum_j|a_j|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $R$ is reflexive and infinite dimensional.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $s=\sum_j a_jr_j$ and $v^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$. Independence gives $\lVert s\rVert_2=v$. Expanding the fourth moment gives
\[
 \mathbb E s^4=3v^4-2\sum_j a_j^4\leq3v^4.
\]
H\"older's inequality gives $\lVert s\rVert_2\leq\lVert s\rVert_1^{1/3}\lVert s\rVert_4^{2/3}$. If $v>0$, this implies $\lVert s\rVert_1\geq v^3/\lVert s\rVert_4^2\geq v/\sqrt3$. The upper bound is $\lVert s\rVert_1\leq\lVert s\rVert_2$. Completion yields an isomorphism onto the closed span of the $r_j$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:Tauberian}
If $T:X\to Y$ has closed range and reflexive kernel, then it is Tauberian.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $Z=\ker T$ and $F=\operatorname{ran} T$. Closedness of $F$ gives a constant $c$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(x,Z)\leq c\lVert Tx\rVert$ for $x\in X$. For each $x^*\in Z^\perp$, the rule $Tx\mapsto x^*(x)$ defines a bounded functional on $F$, and the Hahn--Banach theorem extends it to $Y$. It follows that $\operatorname{ran} T^*=Z^\perp$ and hence
\[
 \ker T^{**}=Z^{\perp\perp}.
\]
Under the natural identification of $Z^{**}$ with $Z^{\perp\perp}\subset X^{**}$, reflexivity gives $Z^{\perp\perp}=J_X Z$.

Suppose that $T^{**}x^{**}=J_Yy$ with $y\in Y$. Every functional annihilating $F$ annihilates $y$, so $y\in F$ by closedness of $F$ and Hahn--Banach separation. Choose $x_0\in X$ with $Tx_0=y$. Then $x^{**}-J_Xx_0\in\ker T^{**}=J_XZ$, so $x^{**}\in J_XX$. The converse inclusion is immediate from $T^{**}J_X=J_YT$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:closed-range}
There exists a bounded operator $\mathcal T:L^1(0,1)\to L^1(0,1)$ with closed range and kernel exactly the usual Rademacher span $R$. It satisfies
\[
 \frac1{2C}\operatorname{dist}(f,R)\leq\lVert \mathcal T f\rVert_1
 \leq5\operatorname{dist}(f,R).
\]
This operator is Tauberian and is not upper semi-Fredholm.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
On the Bernoulli model put
\[
 \mathcal T f=\mathcal I(\mathbb E f,Df),
\]
and use the source identification with $L^1(0,1)$ from Subsection~\ref{sec:infinite}. Proposition~\ref{prop:J} proves the kernel, range, and norm assertions. Lemmas~\ref{lem:R-Hilbert} and~\ref{lem:Tauberian} imply that $\mathcal T$ is Tauberian. An upper semi-Fredholm operator has closed range and finite-dimensional kernel; the latter condition fails here.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:convention}
The operator $D$ annihilates constants as well as $R$. Therefore $f+R\mapsto Df$ alone would not be injective. Formula \eqref{eq:mean-recovery} is the precise reason that adding the single scalar coordinate $\mathbb E f$ suffices. Under the alternative convention in which the constant function belongs to the Rademacher space, the relevant space is $\mathcal A$, and $\widetilde D$ itself is the embedding.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:two-dim}
For the two-dimensional cube take $f=r_1r_2$. Since $|f|=1$ and $\mathbb E(fa)=0$ for $a\in\mathcal A_2$,
\[
 \lVert f-a\rVert_1\geq|\mathbb E((f-a)f)|=1,
 \qquad \operatorname{dist}_{L^1}(f,\mathcal A_2)=1.
\]
If the two swap signs agree, then $D_2f=0$. If they disagree, direct calculation gives
\[
 D_2f=(x_1-y_1)(x_2-y_2).
\]
Thus $|D_2f|=4$ precisely when $x_1\ne y_1$, $x_2\ne y_2$, and $\sigma_1\ne\sigma_2$, an event of probability $1/8$. Consequently $\lVert D_2f\rVert_1=1/2$. Any constant in \eqref{eq:finite-endpoint} must therefore be at least $2$. The much larger value in \eqref{eq:constants} is only an explicit existence bound; no sharpness claim is made.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:coembedding}
If $D:Y\to Z$ satisfies $\lVert Dy\rVert\geq m\lVert y\rVert$ for some $m>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:coembedding}
 \lVert D^{\mathrm{co}}\xi\rVert\geq\tfrac m2\lVert \xi\rVert\qquad(\xi\in Y^{\mathrm{co}}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Put $M=D(Y)$, a closed subspace of $Z$. If $z^{**}\in M^{\perp\perp}$ and $z\in Z$, then
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(z,M)=\sup_{\substack{z^*\in M^\perp\\\lVert z^*\rVert\leq1}}\lvert z^*(z)\rvert
 \leq\lVert z-z^{**}\rVert.
\]
Choosing $m_0\in M$ arbitrarily close to this distance gives
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(z^{**},M)\leq2\operatorname{dist}(z^{**},Z).
\]
The inverse $D^{-1}:M\to Y$ has norm at most $m^{-1}$, and its bidual is defined on $M^{**}=M^{\perp\perp}$. Apply it to $D^{**}y^{**}-m_0$ and take infima. This yields
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(y^{**},Y)\leq m^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(D^{**}y^{**},M)
 \leq2m^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(D^{**}y^{**},Z).
\]
This is \eqref{c:eq:coembedding}. The estimate is the one used in \cite[Proposition~1.4(i)]{GST}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:refquot}
Let $Z$ be a closed reflexive subspace of a Banach space $Y$, and let $q_Y:Y\to Y/Z$ be the metric quotient. Then
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:refquot}
 \ker q_Y^{**}=J_YZ,\qquad
 (q_Y^{**})^{-1}(J_{Y/Z}(Y/Z))=J_YY.
\end{equation}
Moreover $q_Y^{\mathrm{co}}:Y^{\mathrm{co}}\to(Y/Z)^{\mathrm{co}}$ is a surjective isometry.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The adjoint identifies $(Y/Z)^*$ isometrically with $Z^\perp$. Hahn--Banach therefore makes $q_Y^{**}$ a metric quotient with kernel $Z^{\perp\perp}$. Reflexivity gives $Z^{\perp\perp}=J_YZ$.
If $q_Y^{**}y^{**}=J_{Y/Z}x$, choose $y\in Y$ with $q_Yy=x$; then $y^{**}-J_Yy\in J_YZ$. This proves the second assertion in \eqref{c:eq:refquot}.
Finally,
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(q_Y^{**}y^{**},J_{Y/Z}(Y/Z))
 =\inf_{y\in Y}\inf_{z\in Z}\lVert y^{**}-J_Yy-J_Yz\rVert
 =\operatorname{dist}(y^{**},J_YY).
\]
Surjectivity follows from that of $q_Y^{**}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:lifting}
Let $L$ be an $L^1$-space, let $Z$ be a closed reflexive subspace of $Y$, and let $A:L\to Y/Z$ be bounded. There is $\widehat A:L\to Y$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:lifting}
 q_Y\widehat A=A,\qquad \lVert \widehat A\rVert=\lVert A\rVert.
\end{equation}
If $A$ is weakly compact, every bounded lifting of $A$ is weakly compact.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The dual $L^*$ is $1$-injective: it is an $AM$-space with an order unit, hence isometrically a $C(K)$-space by Kakutani's representation theorem, and every dual $C(K)$-space is $1$-injective by \cite[Proposition~4.3.8(i)]{AK16}.
Here $1$-injectivity means that every bounded operator from a subspace of a Banach space into $L^*$ extends to the whole space without increasing its norm.
Identify $(Y/Z)^*$ isometrically with $Z^\perp$ through $q_Y^*$.
The operator $A^*(q_Y^*)^{-1}:Z^\perp\to L^*$ therefore has an extension $B:Y^*\to L^*$ satisfying
\[
 Bq_Y^*=A^*,\qquad \lVert B\rVert=\lVert A\rVert.
\]
Taking adjoints and restricting to $J_LL$ gives
\[
 q_Y^{**}B^*J_L=A^{**}J_L=J_{Y/Z}A.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{c:lem:refquot}, $B^*J_L(L)\subseteq J_YY$. Thus
\[
 \widehat A\coloneqq J_Y^{-1}B^*J_L:L\longrightarrow Y
\]
satisfies $q_Y\widehat A=A$ and $\lVert \widehat A\rVert\leq\lVert A\rVert$.
The reverse inequality follows from $\lVert q_Y\rVert\leq1$.
For any bounded lifting, $q_Y^{\mathrm{co}}\widehat A^{\mathrm{co}}=A^{\mathrm{co}}$.
If $A$ is weakly compact, then $A^{\mathrm{co}}=0$, and injectivity of $q_Y^{\mathrm{co}}$ gives $\widehat A^{\mathrm{co}}=0$.
Gantmacher's criterion completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{c:thm:ALinput}
For $AL$-spaces $L_1,L_2$ and $A\in\mathscr B(L_1,L_2)$,
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:ALinput}
 \lVert A\rVert_w=
 \sup\left\{\frac1{\lVert U\rVert\lVert V\rVert}:
 U:L_2\to\ell_1,\ V:\ell_1\to L_1,\ UAV=\mathrm I_{\ell_1}\right\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{c:cor:ALco}
For an operator $A$ between $AL$-spaces,
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:ALco}
 \lVert A\rVert_w=\lVert A^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For every factorization in \eqref{c:eq:ALinput}, functoriality gives
$U^{\mathrm{co}}A^{\mathrm{co}}V^{\mathrm{co}}=\mathrm I_{\ell_1^{\mathrm{co}}}$.
The space $\ell_1^{\mathrm{co}}$ is nonzero, so
$1\leq\lVert U\rVert\lVert A^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert\lVert V\rVert$.
Take the supremum and use \eqref{c:eq:coineq}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:rad}
The space $R$ is reflexive.
Let $E_N=\mathbb E[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal F_N]$ and $Q_N=E_N|_{R}$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:shrinking}
 Q_Nr_j=\begin{cases}r_j,&j\leq N,\\0,&j>N,\end{cases}
 \qquad\lVert Q_N^*\varphi-\varphi\rVert\longrightarrow0\quad(\varphi\in R^*).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:R-Hilbert} gives an isomorphism $U:\ell_2\to R$, $Ua=\sum_ja_jr_j$, with
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:khintchine}
 3^{-1/2}\lVert a\rVert_2\leq\lVert Ua\rVert_1\leq\lVert a\rVert_2.
\end{equation}
In particular $R$ is reflexive.
Lemma~\ref{lem:conditional} gives the formula for $Q_N$.
The operators $U^{-1}Q_NU$ are the ordinary coordinate projections on $\ell_2$.
Their adjoints converge strongly; conjugation by $U^*$ gives the asserted convergence on $R^*$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:ellone}
There are contractions $j:\ell_1\to X_\mu$ and $p:X_\mu\to\ell_1$ with $pj=\mathrm I_{\ell_1}$. In particular, $P_1=jp$ is an idempotent that is not weakly compact.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
We first work in $X$. The variables $s_k=r_1r_{k+1}$ are independent symmetric signs. Define
\[
 A_n=\{s_1=-1,\ldots,s_{n-1}=-1,\ s_n=1\}.
\]
They are disjoint, have probability $2^{-n}$, and are invariant under $x\mapsto-x$. Thus $\int_{A_n}r_j\,d\mathbb P=0$ for every $n,j$. The formulas
\[
 j_{\Delta}a=q\left(\sum_{n\geq1}a_n\frac{\mathbf 1_{A_n}}{\mathbb P(A_n)}\right),
 \qquad
 p_{\Delta}(qf)=\left(\int_{A_n}f\,d\mathbb P\right)_{n\geq1}
\]
define contractions, and $p_{\Delta}j_{\Delta}=\mathrm I_{\ell_1}$. For $p_{\Delta}$, well-definedness follows by continuity from the vanishing integrals; its norm bound follows from disjointness and infimizing over representatives of $qf$.
Set $j=\bar\iota j_{\Delta}$ and $p=p_{\Delta}\bar P$. Then $pj=\mathrm I_{\ell_1}$, so $j$ is an isometry. If $P_1$ were weakly compact, then $pP_1j=\mathrm I_{\ell_1}$ would be weakly compact, contradicting nonreflexivity of $\ell_1$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:coefficientquotient}
The map
\[
 \mathcal C:L^\infty(\Delta)\to\ell_2,\qquad
 \mathcal Cg=\left(\int_\Delta gr_j\,d\mathbb P\right)_{j\geq1}
\]
is bounded and onto. Each $a\in\ell_2$ has a preimage $g$ with
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:coefficientlift}
 \lVert g\rVert_\infty\leq\sqrt3\lVert a\rVert_2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Bessel gives $\lVert \mathcal Cg\rVert_2\leq\lVert g\rVert_2\leq\lVert g\rVert_\infty$.
The functional $\sum_jc_jr_j\mapsto\sum_jc_ja_j$ has norm at most $\sqrt3\lVert a\rVert_2$ on $R$ by \eqref{c:eq:khintchine}. Extend it to $E$ by Hahn--Banach and represent the extension by $g\in L^\infty$. We use the dual pairing $\int fg$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:bochner}
Let $Z,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $Q:Z\to Y$ be bounded, and suppose every $y\in Y$ admits $z\in Z$ with $Qz=y$ and $\lVert z\rVert\leq c\lVert y\rVert$. For a finite measure $\nu$ and $a\in L^1(\nu;Y)$, there exists $b\in L^1(\nu;Z)$ with
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:bochner}
 Qb(s)=a(s)\text{ almost everywhere},\qquad
 \lVert b\rVert_{L^1(\nu;Z)}\leq2c\lVert a\rVert_{L^1(\nu;Y)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The zero case is immediate. Choose finite-valued simple functions $t_n$ so that
$\lVert a-t_n\rVert_{L^1}\leq\delta2^{-n}$ with $\delta=\lVert a\rVert_{L^1}/2$.
Put $a_1=t_1$ and $a_n=t_n-t_{n-1}$ for $n\geq2$. Then
\[
 a=\sum_{n\geq1}a_n\text{ in }L^1(\nu;Y),\qquad
 \sum_{n\geq1}\lVert a_n\rVert_{L^1}\leq\lVert a\rVert_{L^1}+2\delta=2\lVert a\rVert_{L^1}.
\]
Write each simple $a_n$ on disjoint measurable sets and choose a preimage in $Z$ for each of its finitely many values. This produces a simple $b_n$ with $Qb_n=a_n$ and $\lVert b_n\rVert_{L^1}\leq c\lVert a_n\rVert_{L^1}$.
The series $\sum_nb_n$ converges in the Bochner space $L^1(\nu;Z)$ to the required $b$. Continuity of the induced map on Bochner spaces gives $Qb=a$. No measurable linear right inverse is used.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:boundedkernel}
Let $(S,\nu)$ be a finite measure space and let $h\in L^\infty(S\times\Delta,\nu\otimes\mathbb P)$. Define
\[
 H:E\to L^1(\nu),\qquad
 (Hf)(s)=\int_\Delta h(s,t)f(t)\,d\mathbb P(t).
\]
For every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $C\in\mathscr A(E,L^1(\nu))$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:boundedkernel}
 C|_{R}=H|_{R},\qquad \lVert C\rVert\leq\lVert H\rVert+\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Set $a_j(s)=\int_\Delta h(s,t)r_j(t)\,d\mathbb P(t)$. For almost every $s$, Bessel gives
\[
 \sum_{j\geq1}\lvert a_j(s)\rvert^2
 \leq\int_\Delta\lvert h(s,t)\rvert^2\,d\mathbb P(t)\leq\lVert h\rVert_\infty^2.
\]
Let $a^{>N}(s)$ be the vector with its first $N$ coordinates zero and remaining coordinates $a_j(s)$. These are strongly measurable $\ell_2$-valued functions: their finite-coordinate truncations are measurable and converge pointwise in $\ell_2$. Dominated convergence yields
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:tailfield}
 \lVert a^{>N}\rVert_{L^1(\nu;\ell_2)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Apply Lemmas~\ref{c:lem:coefficientquotient} and~\ref{c:lem:bochner} to obtain
$b_N\in L^1(\nu;L^\infty(\Delta))$ with
\[
 \mathcal Cb_N(s)=a^{>N}(s),\qquad
 \lVert b_N\rVert_{L^1(L^\infty)}\leq2\sqrt3\lVert a^{>N}\rVert_{L^1(\ell_2)}.
\]
Define $B_N:E\to L^1(\nu)$ by
\[
 (B_Nf)(s)=\langle b_N(s),f\rangle.
\]
The scalar function is measurable because evaluation against $f$ is continuous on $L^\infty$, and
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:tailoperator}
 \lVert B_N\rVert\leq\lVert b_N\rVert_{L^1(L^\infty)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Approximating $b_N$ in Bochner norm by finite-valued simple functions approximates $B_N$ in operator norm by finite-rank operators. Thus $B_N$ is approximable; this construction does not require a jointly chosen pointwise representative of every $L^\infty$-class $b_N(s)$.
By construction,
\[
 B_Nr_j=0\ (j\leq N),\qquad B_Nr_j=Hr_j\ (j>N).
\]
Therefore $C_N=HE_N+B_N$ is approximable and agrees with $H$ on every $r_j$, hence on $R$. Since $\lVert HE_N\rVert\leq\lVert H\rVert$, \eqref{c:eq:tailoperator} proves \eqref{c:eq:boundedkernel}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:kernelapprox}
Let the source and target carry finite Borel measures on compact metrizable spaces, with completions allowed. Every weakly compact operator between their $L^1$-spaces is an operator-norm limit of operators with bounded measurable kernels.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Write $H=S+K$ as its singular and integral parts, with kernel $k(s,t)$ for $K$. The cited formula states
\[
 \lVert H\rVert_w
 =\inf_{n\geq1}\operatorname{ess\,sup}_t\left((|S|^*\mathbf 1)(t)
       +\int_{\{|k(s,t)|\geq n\}}\lvert k(s,t)\rvert\,d\nu(s)\right).
\]
For weakly compact $H$ the left side is zero. The nonnegative singular term must vanish, so $S=0$, and the essential suprema of the kernel tails tend to zero. The operators with kernels $k\mathbf 1_{\{|k|<n\}}$ therefore converge to $H$ in norm. The operator-norm estimate needed here follows directly from Tonelli's theorem.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:weakrestriction}
For a finite Borel measure $\nu$ on a compact metrizable space and $H\in\mathscr W(E,L^1(\nu))$, the restriction $H|_{R}$ admits an approximable extension $C:E\to L^1(\nu)$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Choose bounded-kernel operators $H_n$ with $\lVert H-H_n\rVert\leq2^{-n}$, and put $H_0=0$. The series $\sum_{n\geq1}(H_n-H_{n-1})$ converges absolutely in operator norm to $H$.
For each $n$, Lemma~\ref{c:lem:boundedkernel} gives an approximable $C_n$ with
\[
 C_n|_{R}=(H_n-H_{n-1})|_{R},\qquad
 \lVert C_n\rVert\leq\lVert H_n-H_{n-1}\rVert+2^{-n}.
\]
The norm-convergent sum $C=\sum_nC_n$ is approximable, and its restriction to $R$ is $H|_{R}$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:seprange}
If $H:E\to L^1(\mu)$ is bounded, its range is contained in a closed subspace $E_1$ lattice isometric to $L^1(\nu)$ for a standard finite measure $\nu$. The space $E_1$ may be chosen separable. If $H$ is weakly compact into $L^1(\mu)$, it is weakly compact into $E_1$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The zero operator is harmless. Choose a sequence $(f_j)$ dense in $H(E)$ and set
\[
 h=\sum_{j\geq1}2^{-j}\frac{\lvert f_j\rvert}{1+\lVert f_j\rVert_1},\qquad
 A=\{h>0\},\qquad d\nu_0=h\,d\mu\text{ on }A.
\]
The measure $\nu_0$ is finite, and all $f_j$ vanish outside $A$ modulo null sets. Let $\Sigma_1$ be generated on $A$ by the scalar functions $f_j/h$. Multiplication by $h$, followed by zero extension, is a lattice isometry
\[
 L^1(A,\Sigma_1,\nu_0)\longrightarrow L^1(\mu)
\]
whose closed range $E_1$ contains every $f_j$.
Apply the bounded injective transform $u\mapsto (2/\pi)\arctan u$ to the functions $f_j/h$. The resulting countable map takes values in the compact metrizable cube $[-1,1]^{\mathbb N}$ and generates exactly $\Sigma_1$. Its pushforward is a finite Borel measure on that cube; pullback is onto $L^1(A,\Sigma_1,\nu_0)$ by density of simple functions from the generated sigma-algebra. This supplies the required compact-metric model and proves separability.
The weak topology of a closed subspace is the topology induced from the ambient weak topology by Hahn--Banach. A weak closure of a subset of $E_1$ stays in $E_1$, which proves the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{c:prop:initialextension}
Under the ambient condition \eqref{c:eq:ambient}, if $F\in\mathscr W(E_\mu,X_\mu)$, there exists $C_{\mathrm{init}}\in\mathscr A(E,X_\mu)$ with
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:initialextension}
 C_{\mathrm{init}}|_{R}=(F\iota)|_{R}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The subspace $R_\mu$ is reflexive by Lemma~\ref{c:lem:rad}. Lift $F\iota:E\to E_\mu/R_\mu$ through $q_\mu$ by Lemma~\ref{c:lem:lifting}, obtaining a weakly compact $H:E\to E_\mu$. By Lemma~\ref{c:lem:seprange}, regard $H$ as an operator into a standard finite $L^1$-model $E_1$. Lemma~\ref{c:lem:weakrestriction} gives an approximable extension of $H|_{R}$ into $E_1$. Compose it with the inclusion $E_1\to E_\mu$ and $q_\mu$ to obtain $C_{\mathrm{init}}$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{c:thm:maincorrection}
Assume the ambient condition \eqref{c:eq:ambient}. Suppose $G\in\mathscr B(E_\mu,X_\mu)$ and $F\in\mathscr W(E_\mu,X_\mu)$ satisfy $G|_{R_\mu}=F|_{R_\mu}$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $V\in\mathscr A(E_\mu,X_\mu)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:maincorrection}
 V|_{R_\mu}=G|_{R_\mu},\qquad \lVert V\rVert\leq\lVert G\rVert+\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:normimprovement}
Let $Y$ be a Banach space, let $G_{\Delta}:E\to Y$ be bounded, and put $K=G_{\Delta}|_{R}$. If $K$ admits an approximable extension $C_{\mathrm{init}}:E\to Y$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ it admits an approximable extension $V_{\Delta}$ with
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:normimprovement}
 \lVert V_{\Delta}\rVert\leq\lVert G_{\Delta}\rVert+\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Choose a finite-rank operator $A=\sum_{j=1}^k y_j\otimes\varphi_j$ with
$\lVert C_{\mathrm{init}}-A\rVert<\varepsilon/4$, where $\varphi_j\in E^*$.
By \eqref{c:eq:shrinking},
\[
 \lVert \varphi_j|_{R}\circ(\mathrm I_{R}-Q_N)\rVert\longrightarrow0.
\]
Hahn--Banach extends each of these functionals to $\psi_{j,N}\in E^*$ with unchanged norm. Consequently
\[
 L_N=\sum_{j=1}^k y_j\otimes\psi_{j,N}
\]
is finite-rank,
\[
 L_N|_{R}=A|_{R}(\mathrm I_{R}-Q_N),\qquad \lVert L_N\rVert\longrightarrow0.
\]
The operator
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:ZN}
 Z_N=(C_{\mathrm{init}}-A)(\mathrm I_{E}-E_N)+L_N
\end{equation}
is approximable, and
\[
 Z_N|_{R}=K(\mathrm I_{R}-Q_N),\qquad
 \lVert Z_N\rVert\leq2\lVert C_{\mathrm{init}}-A\rVert+\lVert L_N\rVert.
\]
Choose $N$ so that the right side is less than $\varepsilon$. Now put
\[
 V_{\Delta}=G_{\Delta}E_N+Z_N.
\]
The first term is finite-rank, the second approximable, and
\[
 V_{\Delta}|_{R}=KQ_N+K(\mathrm I_{R}-Q_N)=K,
 \qquad
 \lVert V_{\Delta}\rVert\leq\lVert G_{\Delta}\rVert+\varepsilon.
\]
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{c:prop:initialextension} to $F$ and use $F|_{R_\mu}=G|_{R_\mu}$. This gives an approximable extension of $(G\iota)|_{R}$ from $E$ to $X_\mu$. Lemma~\ref{c:lem:normimprovement}, with $G_{\Delta}=G\iota$, produces $V_{\Delta}\in\mathscr A(E,X_\mu)$ satisfying
\[
 V_{\Delta}|_{R}=(G\iota)|_{R},\qquad
 \lVert V_{\Delta}\rVert\leq\lVert G\iota\rVert+\varepsilon\leq\lVert G\rVert+\varepsilon.
\]
Set $V=V_{\Delta}P$. Then $V$ is approximable and $V\iota r=V_{\Delta}r=G\iota r$ for $r\in R$. Contractivity of $P$ proves the claimed norm bound.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:pullbacknorm}
Under the ambient condition \eqref{c:eq:ambient}, for every $T\in\mathscr B(X_\mu)$,
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:pullbacknorm}
 \lVert Tq_\mu\rVert_{w,E_\mu\to X_\mu}=\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Lift $Tq_\mu$ to $A_T:E_\mu\to E_\mu$ with $q_\mu A_T=Tq_\mu$. By Lemma~\ref{c:lem:refquot}, $q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}:E_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}\to X_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}$ is a surjective isometry, and
\[
 q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}A_T^{\mathrm{co}}=T^{\mathrm{co}}q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}.
\]
Thus $\lVert A_T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert=\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert$. By Corollary~\ref{c:cor:ALco},
\[
 \lVert Tq_\mu\rVert_w\leq\lVert A_T\rVert_w=\lVert A_T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert=\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert.
\]
The first inequality follows by composing weakly compact approximants with $q_\mu$. Conversely, \eqref{c:eq:coineq} and surjectivity of $q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}$ give
$\lVert Tq_\mu\rVert_w\geq\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert=\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{c:thm:ambientnorm}
Under \eqref{c:eq:ambient}, every $T\in\mathscr B(X_\mu)$ satisfies
$\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert\leq\lVert T\rVert_w\leq2\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Fix $T\in\mathscr B(X_\mu)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Lemma~\ref{c:lem:pullbacknorm} provides $F\in\mathscr W(E_\mu,X_\mu)$ such that
\[
 \lVert Tq_\mu -F\rVert\leq\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert+\varepsilon.
\]
Put $G=Tq_\mu -F$. Since $q_\mu |_{R_\mu}=0$, we have $G|_{R_\mu}=-F|_{R_\mu}$. Apply Theorem~\ref{c:thm:maincorrection} to $G$ and $-F$, obtaining $V\in\mathscr A(E_\mu,X_\mu)$ with
\[
 V|_{R_\mu}=G|_{R_\mu},\qquad \lVert V\rVert\leq\lVert G\rVert+\varepsilon.
\]
The weakly compact operator $F+V$ vanishes on $R_\mu$, so it factors as $Wq_\mu$ for a bounded $W:X_\mu\to X_\mu$. The operator $W$ is weakly compact: $Wq_\mu$ is weakly compact and $q_\mu$ is a metric quotient. For completeness, $B_{X_\mu}\subset q_\mu (2B_{E_\mu})$, so $W(B_{X_\mu})$ is contained in the relatively weakly compact set $(Wq_\mu)(2B_{E_\mu})$.
The norm identity $\lVert Aq_\mu\rVert=\lVert A\rVert$ for a metric quotient now yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lVert T\rVert_w
 &\leq\lVert T-W\rVert=\lVert (T-W)q_\mu\rVert=\lVert G-V\rVert\\
 &\leq2\lVert G\rVert+\varepsilon
 \leq2\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert+3\varepsilon.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and combine with \eqref{c:eq:coineq}. A bounded-below map from the Banach space $\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)$ has closed range, giving the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{c:prop:algebralift}
Choose any lifting $A_T:E_\mu\to E_\mu$ with $q_\mu A_T=Tq_\mu$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:algebralift}
 \Lambda:\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)\longrightarrow\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(E_\mu),\qquad
 \Lambda([T])=[A_T]
\end{equation}
is a well-defined unital injective homomorphism satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:lambdanorm}
 \lVert \Lambda([T])\rVert=\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert,\qquad
 \tfrac12\lVert [T]\rVert\leq\lVert \Lambda([T])\rVert\leq\lVert [T]\rVert.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Two liftings differ by an operator with range in the reflexive space $R_\mu$, hence by a weakly compact operator. A lifting of a weakly compact $Tq_\mu$ is weakly compact by Lemma~\ref{c:lem:lifting}. These observations prove independence both of the lifting and of the representative $T$.
Sums and scalar multiples of liftings lift the corresponding operators, and
\[
 q_\mu A_TA_U=Tq_\mu A_U=TUq_\mu.
\]
Thus $\Lambda$ is a homomorphism, with $A_{\mathrm I_{X_\mu}}=\mathrm I_{E_\mu}$ available. Its norm equality is proved in Lemma~\ref{c:lem:pullbacknorm}; injectivity and the two-sided bounds follow from Theorem~\ref{c:thm:ambientnorm}.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The proposition is not by itself an inheritance theorem for incompressibility. An embedding of one algebra into an incompressible algebra does not, without further structure, prove incompressibility of its domain. The next subsection supplies the additional quantitative factorization.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{c:lem:globalembedding}
Under the ambient condition \eqref{c:eq:ambient}, the map
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:globalembedding}
 D_\mu:X_\mu\longrightarrow E_\mu\oplus_1F_\Delta,\qquad
 D_\mu(q_\mu f)=\bigl((\mathrm I_{E_\mu}-\iota P)f,\ J(qPf)\bigr)
\end{equation}
is well-defined and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:globalembeddingnorm}
 \lVert x\rVert\leq\lVert D_\mu x\rVert\leq(\kappa+2)\lVert x\rVert.
\end{equation}
Its target is an $AL$-space.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Both components in \eqref{c:eq:globalembedding} vanish on $\iota R$. The quotient retraction \eqref{c:eq:quotretraction} gives
\[
 \lVert q_\mu f\rVert
 \leq\lVert (\mathrm I_{E_\mu}-\iota P)f\rVert+\lVert qPf\rVert
 \leq\lVert D_\mu(q_\mu f)\rVert.
\]
Since $\lVert \mathrm I_{E_\mu}-\iota P\rVert\leq2$ and this operator annihilates $R_\mu$, its induced map from $X_\mu$ has norm at most $2$. Also $\lVert qPf\rVert=\lVert \bar P(q_\mu f)\rVert\leq\lVert q_\mu f\rVert$. These inequalities prove the upper bound. Additivity of the norm on positive elements holds in an $\ell_1$-sum of $AL$-spaces.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{c:prop:criterion}
Assume the ambient condition \eqref{c:eq:ambient}, and suppose $D:X_\mu\to F$ embeds $X_\mu$ into an $AL$-space with
\[
 m\lVert x\rVert\leq\lVert Dx\rVert\leq M\lVert x\rVert\qquad(x\in X_\mu).
\]
Then every bounded injective homomorphism $\Phi:\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)\to B$ into a normed algebra satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:criterion}
 \lVert \Phi(a)\rVert\geq\frac{m}{4M\lVert \Phi\rVert^2}\lVert a\rVert
 \qquad(a\in\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
For $T\in\mathscr B(X_\mu)$ define
\[
 \delta_D(T)=\lVert DTq_\mu\rVert_{w,E_\mu\to F}.
\]
Both $E_\mu$ and $F$ are $AL$-spaces. Hence Corollary~\ref{c:cor:ALco}, Lemma~\ref{c:lem:coembedding}, the isometry $q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}$, and Theorem~\ref{c:thm:ambientnorm} imply
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:deltabound}
 \begin{aligned}
 \delta_D(T)
 &=\lVert D^{\mathrm{co}}T^{\mathrm{co}}q_\mu^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert\\
 &\geq\tfrac m2\lVert T^{\mathrm{co}}\rVert
 \geq\tfrac m4\lVert T\rVert_w.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
There is nothing to prove if $[T]=0$. Otherwise $\delta_D(T)>0$. For $0<\eta<\delta_D(T)$, Theorem~\ref{c:thm:ALinput} gives
\[
 U:F\to\ell_1,\qquad V:\ell_1\to E_\mu,\qquad
 UDTq_\mu V=\mathrm I_{\ell_1},\qquad
 \lVert U\rVert\lVert V\rVert<\frac1{\delta_D(T)-\eta}.
\]
Set $u=UD:X_\mu\to\ell_1$ and $v=q_\mu V:\ell_1\to X_\mu$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{c:eq:transferredfactorization}
 uTv=\mathrm I_{\ell_1},\qquad
 \lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert<\frac{M}{\delta_D(T)-\eta}.
\end{equation}
Use $j,p,P_1$ from Lemma~\ref{c:lem:ellone}, and let $e=[P_1]\in\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)$. It is a nonzero idempotent, and
\[
 [ju]\,[T]\,[vp]=e.
\]
The element $\Phi(e)$ is a nonzero idempotent in $B$, so submultiplicativity gives $\lVert \Phi(e)\rVert\geq1$. Therefore
\[
 1\leq\lVert \Phi\rVert^2\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert\lVert \Phi([T])\rVert.
\]
Using \eqref{c:eq:transferredfactorization} and letting $\eta\downarrow0$, we obtain
\[
 \lVert \Phi([T])\rVert\geq\frac{\delta_D(T)}{M\lVert \Phi\rVert^2}.
\]
Equation~\eqref{c:eq:deltabound} completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{c:thm:ambientalgebra}
Assume \eqref{c:eq:ambient}, with $\kappa$ as in \eqref{c:eq:embinput}.
For every normed algebra $B$ and bounded injective homomorphism $\Phi:\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)\to B$,
\[
 \lVert \Phi(a)\rVert\geq
 \frac{\lVert a\rVert}{4(\kappa+2)\lVert \Phi\rVert^2}\qquad(a\in\mathfrak Q_{\!w}(X_\mu)).
\]
For $X$ the denominator improves to $4\kappa\lVert \Phi\rVert^2$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{c:prop:criterion} to $D_\mu$ from Lemma~\ref{c:lem:globalembedding}, with $m=1$ and $M=\kappa+2$. For $X_\mu=X$ use $D=J$ directly, with $m=1$ and $M=\kappa$. For a contractive $\Phi$, the resulting lower bound is at least $1/[4(\kappa+2)]$, respectively $1/(4\kappa)$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{c:rem:sandwich}
The argument transfers factorizations through $DTq_\mu$; it does not claim that $T\mapsto DTq_\mu$ is an algebra homomorphism. Even when $F=E_\mu$,
\[
 (DTq_\mu)(DUq_\mu)=DT(q_\mu D)Uq_\mu,
\]
which need not be $DTUq_\mu$. Nor is an arbitrary weakly compact approximation to $DTq_\mu$ assumed to annihilate $R_\mu$ or have range in $D(X_\mu)$. The compact correction theorem resolves the needed approximation problem before the sandwich is used.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
